title: Turning a lens on landscapes
text:
Turning a lens on landscapes
Over the past few months, readers might have noticed a number of photos of the American Southwest in this magazine. Staff photographer Melanie Stetson Freeman was behind the lens for all these images. She talked with me about the power of visuals for telling stories about land, nature, and stewardship.
Over the past few months, readers might have noticed a number of photos of the American Southwest in this magazine. We led a recent issue with a shot of the vast, tan Hansel Valley in Utah, the site of a planned data center campus. Another magazine featured sweeping vistas of Grand Staircase-Escalante, the red-rocked national monument that President Donald Trump has moved to dramatically reduce in size. And this week, our story about the dwindling water levels in Lake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir, shows breathtaking expanses of dry canyon plunging to a shrinking, narrow ribbon of teal green.
Staff photographer Melanie Stetson Freeman was behind the lens for all these images. She and staff writer Story Hinckley traveled together throughout the region to work on a series of environmental stories, which Mel says are among her favorites to report – in no small part because of the importance of visuals for storytelling.
“A lot of these stories we’ve been doing are about these big open lands that don’t have any human buildings or even evidence of people,” Mel told me. “You want to show the beauty of that land, which is a big part of the story.”
To illustrate scale, Mel says, she looks for objects that might give a sense of perspective – a person, a rock, or, as in her Hansel Valley cover shot, a fence line. And to find the right location for a shot, she often relies on local guides like Beth Henshaw, who in this issue brought Story and Mel to an overlook where they could capture the expanse of red rock and a “bathtub ring” that shows where the lake’s water once reached.
“Water is going to become such a huge issue for so many people,” Mel says. “This particular story of the Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell – it’s visually so obvious.”
That obviousness takes many forms: the challenge of water management, the pressing need for interpersonal and governmental collaboration, the opening for new solutions. Story writes about all of those in her piece this week.
What’s also obvious from Mel’s photography is the solemnity of these places and the humanity of those living and working within them.
We hope you take a moment to sit with these images.
